title: Namdev close
hook: a low-caste printer whose songs sit inside the Guru's book, named by a Guru as one who found freedom

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sultan's demand: raise the dead cow, or else, and Namdev saying nothing happens by his doing. Your line was saved, not shown. Did you choose the honest thing over the impressive one? Day seven hundred seventy-three.

Namaa chheeba. Namdev the printer. That's how a Sikh Guru names him in a hymn, by his trade, the very thing some people of his day held against him. The Guru doesn't hide it or polish it. He says it plainly, and then says what Namdev found. Five days we've spent with this cloth printer: his tools, his cup of milk, the temple at his back, the thread through the beads, the sultan's threat. Today we close his pages by hearing how the Gurus heard him.
screen: `NAMDEV THE PRINTER.` → `NAMED BY HIS TRADE.` → `HOW THE GURUS HEARD HIM.`

segments.voice: The line is in Sri Raag, on Ang 67, in a hymn of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru. In paraphrase: Namdev the printer and Kabir the weaver found liberation through the perfect Guru. They recognized the Word, and their ego and their caste fell away. Hear what that sentence does. It starts with two working men, named by work that others ranked low. And it ends with freedom. Caste isn't argued with. It just falls away, like a label that no longer has anything to stick to. Now gather Namdev's week into that line. At his printing table, his mind was the measuring yard and his tongue the scissors, and he asked what caste and lineage had to do with the Name. He set down a cup of milk and pleaded until the Lord drank. Thrown out of a temple, he sang at the back wall, and the temple turned. With a string of beads he showed the One thread through everything. And bound before a sultan, he refused to perform and said nothing happens by his doing. Every scene is low to the ground. A workbench, a cup of milk, the back of a building, a prisoner's place. And in each one, the song ends higher than where it began. Sikhs sing his hymns as gurbani, the Guru's word. A printer whose caste was counted low, and whose songs now sit in the Guru's own book. Low caste, high song.
screen: `THE PRINTER AND THE WEAVER.` · `EGO AND CASTE FALL AWAY.` · `A WEEK OF LOW PLACES.` · `HIS SONGS IN THE GURU'S BOOK.` · then, large: `LOW CASTE, HIGH SONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a humble worker. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone whose work keeps your day running and who is rarely thanked. The person who cleans the building. The driver. The cook. The one who stocks the shelves at night. Picture their hands at work, the way Namdev's hands worked the cloth. Hold them in your mind with respect for a few breaths. Then decide how you'll honor them today: their name learned, a real thank you, a kindness they didn't expect. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
Namdev close. The printer named by his trade in Guru Amar Das's hymn, whose caste fell away and whose songs sit in the Guru's book.
Your line: low caste, high song. Today, learn the name of one person whose work you usually walk past, and use it. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Namdev's hymns in kirtan as gurbani, and the Gurus' naming of Namdev and Kabir by their trades is often recalled when Sikhs speak about the rejection of caste.
